What that results in, is different hedge profiles across the Group. For example, in recent past we've observed that deposits in UK Corporate Bank have been comparatively more rate sensitive than Barclays UK and that does impact the structure and ongoing management of hedging. Finally, on USCB, now that this division is stand-alone you will see FX impacts more clearly as we did during Q324. We'll continue to call such impacts out when relevant. In addition, you should also be able to see clearer seasonality trends. So Q3 was impacted by higher rewards earned by customers through increased spend, but we do expect these factors to be less of a headwind going into Q4 due to higher holiday spend. And we continue to target a NIM of greater than 12% by 2026, driven by a number of actions. Firstly we've completed the repricing actions on our cards, this will drip-feed through to NIM over time once customers purchase under the new terms and conditions. Secondly, the funding mix, as at Q3 USCB core deposits were 66% of its funding base and we want that to be above 75% by 2026. This will take time to build, but we have now launched the tiered savings products that will underpin that. speaker: Anna Cross
text: Okay, thank you. So just to remind everybody, Tesco in isolation, has a high cost income ratio. So, £360 million of costs against £400 million of NII. On revenue upside from Tesco, I would say this pertains not just to the Tesco customers, I think it comes from a couple of things. It comes from, as you say, funding benefit, but it also comes from our ability to reach out to a different customer set and build relationships with them that are more broad than the existing products that Tesco offers. speaker: Anna Cross

speaker: Ben Toms
text: Good morning, Ben Toms from RBC. Firstly on the structural hedge, how should we think about the notional this year? I think it fell 6% in 2024. Should we expect a further decline but at a slightly lower rate or is flat the right way to think about it? And the duration increased in 2024. Should we expect that to kind of stay flat from here or should it increase a bit further? And then secondly, last week, you guided that you'd expect costs to be down in 2026 over 2025. I think your restructuring run rate is something like £200 to £300 million per annum, but you also mentioned in your opening remarks about if the opportunity presents itself, you would accelerate the plan. Could the underlying restructuring rate pick up a bit this year or is the fall in 2026 driven by actions that we're already aware of. Thank you.

speaker: Anna Cross
text: Okay, thank you. I might ask Dan to pick up on the first one, but I'll answer the second one to give him a moment. So yes, what we talked about last week was actually our target is a circa 61% cost income ratio for this year and for it to fall to the high 50s next year in 2026. The way I see that in absolute terms is for it to go up in the current year, I think consensus is broadly in the right place and then fall back towards circa £17 billion in 2026. And really, there are three things that I've got in mind, which are the things I called out at last week's events. So they are inflation, which is more intense than 2025 than it is in 2026. That's just because the headline rate is coming down and clearly we experienced that headline rate on a delayed basis and there's some, not one off, but more unusual things in the current year like the increase in National Insurance costs. The second is the rate of change of our investment really is more intense than 2025 than it is in 2026. And what I mean by that is we've picked up the run rate of investment in the second half of the year. And you see that particularly, not just in Barclays UK where they've been taking some additional cost as we prepare for Tesco, but also in Private Bank and Wealth Management and in the UK Corporate Bank. So you saw that uptick and you see a full year of that investment. But most meaningfully, it's Tesco and the addition of the £360 million of costs and then integration costs on top. There's not a meaningful change as we go into 2026, and in fact, what we expect to start to see is some cost benefits coming from Tesco, as the integration proceeds. And all the while, we've got a gross efficiency programme, which is continuing to run, we did £1 billion last year. We've got circa £500 million in gross efficiency savings this year and circa £500 million next year. So the relative weightings of those two things push costs cost up in 2025 and should pull them down in 2026. The £200 to £300 million per annum [of structural cost actions], absent 2023, has been an ongoing level that you would expect us to run. In 2024, we were towards the top end of that and it was quite skewed towards the back end, which is why we called it out because it certainly caused some variance to the consensus in the fourth quarter. From our perspective, we see that as normal, so I wouldn't call out anything particular at this point in time. But what you should expect us to do is to operate within the guidance that we've given you. So if we did see the opportunity to accelerate plans or secure the 2026 number, provided that doesn't compromise 2025, then we would consider that as an opportunity. Circa 61% for 2025 is all in, including the increase that I'm talking about in terms of Tesco. Dan, do you want to talk about the structural hedge?

speaker: Dan Fairclough
text: So we gave you some guidance obviously at the beginning of the year on the expectations of the roll of the structural hedge. And we said 75%, sort of illustratively, is what we were looking at. That's exactly really what we saw in 2024, for 75% of the balances we rolled into the structural hedge. So we'll obviously keep a close eye on this, depending on how we see deposit stability progress from here, but at this point I don't think we'd change that view in terms of what we expect. Obviously with the shape of the yield curve at the moment, you know there's actually relatively limited difference from an NII perspective, in terms of the balances, floating versus fixed. But obviously the structural hedge size will determine the stability and the locked in nature of the income going forward. In terms of the duration, I mean it's relatively small changes in duration and those duration changes were really in response to increasing signs of deposit stability that we saw. And this is the way we look at it, and we very much react to the customer behaviour that we're seeing. So it's possible that we'll get a little bit more stability and therefore a little bit of extension, but I think it will be pretty modest really.

speaker: Alvaro Serrano
text: Hello, Alvaro Serrano from Morgan Stanley. A couple of questions on the themes that you've already touched on, but hopefully with a new angle. On the US cards, to get to $40 billion, you have to grow balances. If I take out American Airlines and add General Motors, about 40% or a bit more than 40%. Putting Basel 3.1 end game aside, my impression is there's an expectation that CCAR is going to be watered down. Can you help us think through how that would help you? It's obviously less capital, but is that for the Group? Is it a constraint? What would you do in that scenario? What possibly does that open up? Thank you.

speaker: Anna Cross
text: Okay, thank you, Alvaro. So let me touch on the US cards to start with and then we'll come to CCAR. And again, Dan might want to make some comments on the closeout of that question. So in the plan that we have, the majority of the growth, more than [two thirds] we assume was organic, so that is our objective. Within there, we do typically expect a number of partners over any particular planning period. It's also important to think about how we retain partners. So if I just take those in turn, I mean General Motors at around $2 billion is the kind of size and scale of partner that we are pleased to bring on, between $2 and $4 billion. It is really an ideal size, both in terms of the implementation and the integration of it, but also the concentration that it places within the portfolio. So expect us to be focused on both of those two things. In terms of the NIM, I wouldn't expect it to be linear. There are factors within there that will be a bit more linear. So I would call out the funding benefits that we expect to see as we continue to build out the deposit franchise and the repricing actions that we've taken already. They're already in the terms and conditions for those customers, but they have to purchase on those new terms and conditions for that NIM impact to draw through, which is why you're going to see it drift through over time. So I'd expect those two things to be more linear. There are other things which will be less [linear]. The first will be a degree of seasonality in the business. You can see that in the fourth quarter, you probably see it in the first quarter also, and then you tend to see a little bit lower as you go into the middle of the year, just running in line with borrowing behaviour in the US, remember that post-holiday season, we see a pay down, you get tax credits in the US, people use those. So there's just a natural ebb and flow to the NIM that we would expect. And then the other thing would be, as we sort of rebalance the portfolio away from the super prime travel portfolio that we have, towards more retail, both by growing the partners we already have but also the opportunity to bring on new ones. Then you should see that NIM change. I mean one of the things that we said about American Airlines is we've had a long partnership with them, a long relationship with them. That's not just actually in US cards but in the Investment Bank as well. So it's certainly a relationship that we are sorry to see go, but at the same time it's got a low risk adjusted margin. And so over time, I would hope that the portfolios that we bring on would push that risk adjusted margin up. Moving on to your second point, it's difficult to speculate about regulatory change in the US because there's clearly been a lot of commentary and we have yet to see anything formal either in terms of CCAR, or indeed in terms of Basel 3.1. So take these general comments before then. We typically perform well in CCAR because we've got a diversified business in the US. To the extent that it's watered down, it would reduce the overall capital levels that we've got in the US, but Dan, you might want to add.

speaker: Dan Fairclough
text: Generally, we operate in a position where the Group and the PRA metric is more binding on us than the legal entity capital metrics. So, certainly a watering down of CCAR would give us great flexibility in terms of capital and how we deploy it across our legal entities. But more important is the regulation and the Bank of England stress test. So it is helpful, but it's not a key driver for us.

speaker: Sheel Shah

speaker: Anna Cross
text: Okay, thank you for those. The first is quite difficult to answer really, without seeing the details of the portfolios that come up, but you should expect us, as we said, to want to do more in retail proportionately. The retail market and the travel and entertainment markets in the US are broadly the same scale. We've got a good market share in travel, I think it's around 12% from memory and a much lower, low single digit share in retail. So you should expect us to sort of be biased towards that retail side. That being said, we are very focused on the credit quality of this portfolio. You've seen over time actually, even though we've had different portfolios within there, the FICO of this business overall has been about 740 for a long time. So when I talk about a slight movement in our expectation of risk, it's not a massive wholesale change there at all. We have a relatively conservative risk appetite for this business and actually, one of the things that really works here is where we are providing consumer banking services to existing Investment Banking clients. That works extremely well for us, the Group, and again, you've seen us do that through last year. A good example is Wyndham, a long standing Investment Banking client and we renewed that early, directly with Wyndham and that one didn't actually go to market. So that breadth of relationship is important to us. In terms of single issuer, there are a small number of very large programmes in the US, so Costco, Walmart, Delta, American, and typically they do go to single issuers. Things of that scale are unlikely to be of interest to us, just because of the concentration risk associated with them. We have an appetite to grow this business, but it's capital hungry as we said, you know, we want to be able to share that risk with external partners as we went through in 2024. We can see that business being $40 billion, but I can't see it necessarily being $100 billion, put it that way. Okay, thank you.

speaker: Amit Goel
text: Hi, thank you. Amit Goel from Mediobanca. I've also got some follow-ups, just on the USCB business. And then secondly, if you give a little bit of colour in terms of the RWA regulatory impact, where I guess the estimate was unchanged post the AA piece changing. So just curious the moving parts there or how you're thinking that's going to be repaid? So that's just on the AA part. And I had a second question just on the BUK fee line, I just wanted to just check in terms of what you're thinking. I think the guidance is for greater than 250 million per quarter. Obviously that's a step down versus the kind of Q3 / Q2 rate, but better than Q4, which was impacted by securitisation. Just wanted to just get a sense of how much should I anticipate ongoing securitisation type effects? And how to think about that line going forward? Thanks.

speaker: Anna Cross
text: Okay. Thank you. Okay, it's definitely cards day today. So USCB, how do we get to mid-teens [RoTE]? Well, I think about four factors there. The first is NIM that we talked about this morning already. So the repricing that we've done already and the funding costs are the major factors there. And also this move towards a higher risk adjusted return more generally, as we morph the portfolio and rebalance it away from being quite travel and entertainment dominant. The second one is volume, as I've talked about here, you've got a relatively fixed cost base. You know a good example of that is with GM. I said we're not going to have to rebuild all the capability that we had to do for GAP. So you've got the ability, as you onboard more volume, your marginal cost comes down across the complex. The third is capital efficiency. So you're right, clearly we have some degree of regulatory drag here from the IRB model. So you should expect us to pursue further opportunities for capital and risk sharing with external parties as we did in Q1 with Blackstone which was successful. You should imagine that we're going to do that again. Finally, costs. It's really interesting to reflect on where this business has come from, as we think about its efficiency. You know, if you're running travel files with thousands of dollars per account, your ability to handle that manually is significantly higher. As you move into an environment where you inherently have smaller balances per account, you want to be more and more digital. So if I look at the digital interactions in that business, they're at 93%. Now that's improved, we expect that to improve by a further 10% this year. If I contrast it to BUK, I mean BUK would be 98 / 99% in comparison. Now you might say, well BUK is not a good comparison because it's clearly a retail bank, and therefore you're going to have current account activities that are [generally] higher, but actually our German cards business wasn't that different. So we do think there's an opportunity here for us to increase, not only the efficiency of the business, but actually the customer experience by making more of the activity digital. So it's really through those four steps that we think we can get to, first, in line with the Group. And then secondly, pushing on to the mid-teens [RoTE]. And then in terms of the $16 billion, it remains our best estimate and the reason I say that is of course, we are expecting AA to fall out of the portfolio, but I'm also expecting other things to go back in. And the thing that's somewhat uncertain is the timing. We know the timing of when we will have built that model by, but the timing of the approval of that model and therefore the implementation that I would expect to follow that. Typically, once we've got approval around the model, it takes us around six months say to implement it. So it's the timing really. So the exact size and shape of that portfolio at the point of implementation is not entirely clear at this point in time, which is why we're saying the best estimate we have is the one that we previously had, which is we would expect the portfolio to be about the same size. And then finally on your question on BUK fees. This line does move around a little bit because you've got a few things going on there. You've clearly got securitisations, you've got debt sales and various other bits and pieces. The best estimate I can give you is greater than 250, which is what we said in in the past. I wouldn't expect a lot of securitisation in this business. And Dan might want to comment on this. This is part of the portfolio that we have around risk transfer. It's at a true sale risk transfer. So expect us to do it episodically, as we dynamically manage the balance sheet, but Dan you might want to add.

speaker: Dan Fairclough
text: I think periodic is the right sort of thinking. Obviously the one in Q4 was specifically on a particular bit of the mortgage books, stage 2, stage 3 loans. And we'll do that on occasion, just to make sure that the risk profile is in the right place.

speaker: Anna Cross
text: But again, we'll call out, you know, as and when we expect to do so.

speaker: Amit Goel
text: Does the greater than 250 reflect some of those further actions?

speaker: Anna Cross

text: So in terms of 2025 costs, I would say I'm comfortable with the total. So to the extent that we continue to actively acquire as we have been doing in the market, I would expect that to be less impactful. The specific impact of bringing on new partners, it depends. So in some cases, you're bringing on a back book where you've already got a portfolio which is earning at a reasonable RoTE, as we did, for example with GAP. And then there are some like Breeze, they start from scratch. So it depends on the specific pathway. In terms of RoTE aspirations for 2027 versus 2026, I'm clearly not going to give you additional guidance here, but you should tell from our overall tone that 2026 is not, we believe, a resting place. We're ambitious for the business and we want to keep pushing the RoTE on a consistent basis upwards.

text: Thanks so much. Can I come back to the whole issue of growth and I guess growth in the UK economy, growth in your lending. It's obviously a huge theme with the new government. And I was talking to one of your peers last week. I don't want to put words in their mouth, but broadly speaking, they were saying there's nothing the government could do because there's no demand. So, however much regulation changes doesn't make any difference, which I guess the government will be quite surprised by. speaker: Anna Cross
text: Good question Ed, one that we've discussed actually with quite a few in investors on the road. You know we remain optimistic about our ability to grow within the UK economy. In part, because we are pushing on areas where we have lost market share. Or indeed didn't have it, for example, like High Loan to Value mortgages. You can see that in our ability to pull in additional volumes in cards. I mean, [bringing on 1] million [new] cards is the most cards we have written since 2012, in this environment. And that was actually through us improving our customer journey. So this is not just all about pricing and risk, it's actually about the ease in which you interact with your customers. The same is very much true about our corporate customers, if you recall what Matt [Hammerstein] was talking about when he did his deep dive on the UK Corporate Bank. The first is, 2026 was designed to be a point in time. We gave you a three-year plan, it's not deemed to be an ending point for any of the metrics that we set out for you, whether that was RoTE, whether that was the proportion of capital deployment. The plan had the ultimate aim of raising the returns of the Group and making them more consistent and we believe that is driven by deploying a greater proportion of capital in the Group towards the higher returning, more stable businesses. That plan remains intact. So I wouldn't see the 50% or the 12% as being a resting point, you should expect them to progress beyond that. I'm not going to give you numbers now, I can't give you the endpoint. Think of it as a sense of direction and momentum that we would expect it to continue. Really importantly for us, we see value in having a diversified business that allows us particularly to perform in a range of environments, but we have to get the right capital balance across the Group and we're on a journey. 2026 is a staging point, that is the one that we are 100% focused on delivering right now and we'll come back to you in due course. speaker: Anna Cross
text: Let me start with UK NII. I think a hockey stick is too strong an expression. You know, clearly what we called out is that there was some headwinds in NII in the first couple of quarters really from these maturing swaps. The timing on the accounting, which then neutralises in the second half. And remember you've also had some base rate reduction effects in the first half as well, so, you get that sort of repricing timing coming through. So specifically what you should be modelling is that the negative factor in product margin in that sort of diagram that we've given you goes from being negative to neutral to positive essentially in the second half. So, I'm not looking at any particular lumpiness. Really what you've got coming through is continued role of the structural hedge, continued asset growth, but then the margin matter, really that hedge effect dissipating and also the maturation of cards starting in the second half. So not lumpy. On the second point on cards, it's difficult to call out a specific percentage. Essentially, what stage two is that's the real sort of procyclical element of IFRS 9 is the way I think about it. Because they're almost certainly not delinquent, but your model is telling you given the macroeconomic environment or your macroeconomic assumptions that they may well become delinquent and therefore you start providing for those. So, there can be movements in and out of stage one and stage two purely on the basis of a change in consensus, macroeconomic consensus, which we use to drive our IFRS9 models. So, it's difficult to call out a specific percentage, but if you saw an expected deterioration in the macroeconomic environment, that's where you'd see the increase in charge coming through a higher coverage of those stage two balances. The other thing I would say is perhaps two offsetting things. Given that the level of indebtedness is such structurally lower, not just in the UK but in the US, clearly that also feeds into whether someone is stage one or stage two. Because the more sort of borrowings you have, the more likely it is that we regard you as a stage two borrower. So, a general level of reduction in indebtedness across both markets will feed through into a generally lower level. Conversely to that, if you start to see a pickup in spending that comes from economic confidence, even though the environment might be better, if customers start spending more, then that can also trigger them into stage two. I often say to my colleagues, if they go and buy a new house and start buying stuff for the house, they will certainly become a stage two customer irrespective of whether or not you feel you are a credit risk. So, it's quite sensitive really to nuances and customer behaviour. So, I won't call out percentage but a few things to think about there. And then finally in terms of the US cards book we continue to look for new partners in the US and you should expect us to do so. We see really our sweet spot probably where we have a competitive edge around a slightly smaller portfolio, say between £2-4 billion. We like that because typically, it doesn't put a huge concentration in our book, which we're always mindful of. So, we don't want very, very large books within there, just because of the scale of our business. So don't expect us to pursue a Walmart or a Costco or anything like that. Simply the book isn't big enough to house that. We wouldn't want the concentration risk. It is always a balance between price and the rest of the service that you can give those businesses. Remember for us we do not have our own brand in terms of cards. That makes a difference to partners. We are not competing in the wallet against them with our own card. The other thing is we carry their brand. So the service and the operational stability that goes with it is really important. So we continue to invest in digitisation of this business. And in fact, the customer facing and customer engagement digitisation is probably the best in the business, not necessarily at the operational end, but in the way that you interact with us. So we think that's also important for partners. So it's not just price, it's very multifaceted. And you can see that in our retention. In the last year we've won not only the GM, but we've retained four. So, it does come through in the retention stats. We're able to build those businesses very successfully, retain clients, provide a really high level of service. And you can see that in the satisfaction of the partners that we work with. So very focused on that.

text: Hello everybody. Thank you so much for joining us in the middle of what I know is a really busy day for all of you and for the market, so really appreciate you coming along. As always, let me start with some reflections on the key themes from our discussions on the road over the last few days. But let me start first with the reflections on the Q3 results. So, whilst the absolute RoTE has clearly improved, we have had some questions on whether or not our capital discipline in relation to the IB has affected our relative performance. The simple answer is no, and actually we've seen good performance in some of the areas of the Investment Bank that are inherently more capital intensive. Specifically in DCM, we grew our year-to-date share in Leverage Finance by about 20 basis points year-on-year, and we've participated in 13 of the top 20 global deals in the quarter. And then in FICC, we performed broadly in line with our peers despite not having commodities and with a smaller footprint in Securitised Products. And I think both of those two things were called out across the market in Q3. We did, however, call out areas where we do need to do better and they do overlap with our existing focus businesses that we talked to you about a few times now. That includes, Corporate M&A and ECM, both of those are capital light. And in Equity Derivatives, our limited presence in Asia and not having a captive retail and wealth offering, where activity has been strong across the market, was a relative headwind for us. I think the other thing I would say is, capital discipline remains really important for us, and we do believe that there are further opportunities for capital efficiency within the IB complex. Broadly, there is nothing that happened in Q3 that undermines that strategy addressing some other specific items in the quarter. We hope our Private Credit disclosure has been useful. However, as we've got on the road, ABS Financing has also been a focus area given Tricolor. Our ABS franchise is market leading. It's mature and it's scaled and it's predominantly in the US, and a lot of what we said about risk management and how we manage risk in Private Credit is directly attributable to the ABS business. The risks from the business arises from the collateral that we fund but has not yet been distributed and we manage that in a number of ways. First, we are protected from first losses via senior funding. Second, we have long running, very granular and high frequency credit performance data, and what that allows us to do is proactively and appropriately size the credit protection and adjust the collateral if we feel it is necessary. Thirdly, more than 80% of the consumer related exposures that are structured, are structured to double A or better and less than 3% is below single A. So now moving on to the transaction that we announced this morning, as you know, we have a clear capital hierarchy and a high bar for investment. Best Egg meets that high bar by adding scale and capability at the right price, generating a return on investment that is comparable to the three highest returning UK businesses over time and being accretive to both the US Consumer Bank and Group RoTE from 2027. As a Group matter, our distribution commitments are unaffected. In fact, we expect a circa 6 basis point net release of capital across the sale of American Airlines and the acquisition of Best Egg. So, what is it? Simplistically, it's a direct-to-consumer provider of US personal loans. This is a market that we already participate in, but we lacked the capability to do it at scale. It is an originate to distribute model and the loans are distributed through forward flow arrangements, sourcing consumer credit for alternative asset managers, and also through securitisations, transferring risk and retaining a modest vertical slice of the structure. We expect the acquisition to be accretive to USCB RoTE from 2027 and to support its mid-teens RoTE target in the medium term. And it does so in three ways. First, it replaces the majority of the scale lost through the loss of the American Airlines business, and with the General Motors book acquisition, we will broadly replace all of the American Airlines income, and the income that we gain comes from higher quality origination and servicing fees through non-NII. And it therefore generates a higher RoTE. Second, it improves USCB's capital efficiency. Best Egg loans are distributed to its funding partners and do not attract material credit risk RWAs, allowing us to grow in a capital efficient way. Whilst we expect to retain some personal loans, these attract a lower risk weight than for US cards, and this will continue to be the case post-AIRB. Third, Best Egg offers synergies with the existing business. It expands our capabilities to originate personal loans directly to consumers beyond our existing offering. And these capabilities will help enhance our proposition for co-brand partners and customers. Moreover, we are able to leverage the capabilities and relationships in the Investment Bank, given the overlap between Best Egg's funding partners and our Investment Bank clients and SRT investors. As a final comment, I want to stress that Best Egg customers are prime, with an average FICO score of around 710 and delinquency rates consistently below the peer average. And whilst we may retain some additional loans in the future, I would expect that the average FICO scores for those to be higher and to exceed 725. So with that, I'm happy to take your questions.

So, we remain comfortable where we are positioned and we do see it as sustainable in terms of the pricing. I mean the other things that are directly impacting the NIM are the growth in retail deposits. Remember there's a 50 to 60 basis points differential there [versus wholesale lending] and also the general expansion towards retail balances. Now, clearly in the quarter, there's only been one month of General Motors. So revenue sharing arrangements, I'm not going to call any of them out. We never do as a partner matter and they do actually impact both the NIM line and the non-NII line. So that's why you're seeing some improvements there also, as well as there being just generally increased volumes. So, underlying your question, is this sustainable? The answer is yes, we do believe it is, which is why we said we expected NIM to be broadly stable from here. Just remember it is quite a seasonal business, so you get some lumps and bumps particularly in Non-NII. So we're happy with that general direction. If I go onto the Investment Bank, what you've seen for the last six quarters is that the revenue over RWAs continues to improve. So, if you look year-over-year across those six quarters, you can see a step change each time and clearly what we were looking for at the beginning of the plan was the area where revenue over RWAs had declined markedly over time, [which] was really in the Banking business. And that's where we see a lot of the improvements starting to come through in very, very good capital discipline in driving that Treasury Coverage model. So, you can see that in the International Corporate Bank balances that are growing, and the income there, but also really being focused in M&A and ECM and as I called out before, we do feel there's more to go in those businesses. So in terms of the Banking business, you would expect there to be further road to travel in terms of this revenue over RWAs, because of the International Corporate Bank business continuing to perform. Just because we still have ambitions within ECM and M&A, that they remain a focus for us, but also just this kind of real discipline about the maturation of capital and really whether we continue to extend it to that client or not, or choose to put it elsewhere. So much more to go, I think tangibly within Banking. But in the Markets business, clearly that was coming from a slightly different place. It wasn't a situation where we deployed more capital into that business and that it had largely maintained its revenue over RWAs. What you're seeing now is it continuing to improve because it is taking share, and in many instances we'd already given capital to those focus businesses and they're sort of growing into the capital and maturing into that capital. And then the other thing is obviously Financing, a very capital light business, continues to grow, particularly on the Prime side where the balances were 30% up year on year. So, I can't give you a specific target and indeed that's not how we're thinking about this business in particular, because we do think of it in terms of RoTE. So, it's a number of things to get there, but think of us as still feeling like there's room to go in terms of that revenue over RWAs.

Starting with funding synergies. Again, remember that's what we did in Tesco, they're the ones that normally come through first and I called those out before. Remember, this isn't a bank at the moment. So, there are clear funding synergies in terms of the pre-securitisation position, the cost of securitisation itself. Then you come to cost synergies, for a while we would expect to run this as a business in parallel and then incur the integration over time. So I wouldn't call out any particular integration chunks next year, but clearly, we'll update you on that. But funding is a key point. speaker: Anna Cross
text: Our Financing business is working well and remember this comes in two parts. So, our Fixed Income Financing business, very much embedded in the heritage of Barclays and Lehman before it. It is typically number one or two in the market. So very, very well-established business. What we've been doing is growing Prime alongside that. We've gone from typically number seven or eight to joint number five. So, we've clearly made some progress there. As you note, our targeting has been with the larger of the hedge funds, that's deliberate, and it reflects both our business model and our view of risk. So by business model, what I mean is we run our Financing business as an integrated business. So Fixed Income Financing and Prime are run under a single leadership. So when we approach a client, that's how we approach them, not as two individual businesses. We also run our technology that way. So, as we're looking at those clients, we look across their business in its totality, and we believe that gives us a better perspective of their risk. That lends itself to the largest global multi-strategy type funds, so that's really why you see that approach. But also, in terms of our own risk positioning, we do believe that, again, the first step in risk management is through the careful selection of clients, and therefore we choose to work with the larger, more capitalised, more liquid clients in the industry. That's really where we prefer to operate. That may mean that we give up a little margin along the way, but that certainly is a risk matter where we would want to operate. So, it's a deliberate strategy. So, from our perspective, we would want to grow as they do. Clearly, we do feel there's more for us to do there. Thank you so much. Really appreciate you coming in again on a very busy day in the market. So, appreciate your time and questions, particularly on Best Egg. We will see you on the 10th of February, if not before. Thank you very much.

text: Thank you, Anna. Barclays is now on a journey to sustainably higher returns. I think of this journey as taking place in four stages. First, from 2021 to '23 we stabilised the bank's financial profile, exercising capital discipline in the Investment Bank while starting to build on areas of strength. Second, since the launch of our Simpler, Better and More balanced strategy in February '24 we have positioned the bank for income growth and for higher returns. We have simplified our processes to drive efficiency, and we exited non-strategic businesses. We have invested in digital capabilities to create a better customer experience. And we have grown our highest returning UK businesses to create a More balanced Barclays, with more stable returns. Today we set out the third stage of this plan, on the way to the fourth. In this third stage, we will build on the foundations we have created so far to increase returns for the bank and to make them resilient across a range of environments. Year by year we are improving the profit signature of the bank. Stronger financial results create the capacity to invest to secure sustainably higher returns. This is our fourth stage and it extends beyond 2028. text: Our confidence in the plan that Venkat outlined reflects three factors. First, we plan on realistic assumptions to put delivery in our control. Second, the plan includes a significant increase in discretionary investment to support future growth. In doing so, we are intentionally prioritising sustainably higher long term returns over stronger shorter-term RoTE. And third, that delivery is grounded in existing momentum. For example, target income CAGR of more than 5% compares to 7% delivered since '23, as you can see on the top row. Planned UK lending growth of more than 5% is in line with the momentum seen in '25. And we expect Investment Bank income to RWAs to increase by more than 40 basis points to greater than 7%, having increased 110 basis points in the last two years. Our planning assumption is for a low-single digit IB income CAGR '25 to '28, versus 9% achieved so far and I will come back to this in more detail. The low 50s target cost: income ratio in '28 represents more of a step change. speaker: Kian Abouhossein
text: Two questions. The first question is on the capital return of over £15 billion. If you could just put this in context of capacity to support investment and growth. How should we think about this capacity that you're outlining? It looks like there's quite a bit of buffer. So we would like to understand that. And then secondly, you're one of the few CEOs who actually discusses ledgers and middle office integration, which is not a hot topic. But trying to understand a little bit the investment phase, which has stepped up in 2026 significantly and you're going from £1.1 billion to £2.3 billion of investments. Just what the focus is and how should we think about post 2028 basically in that respect?

speaker: C.S. Venkatakrishnan
text: Anna, do you want to start on the capital and then we can come back to the other one?

speaker: Anna Cross
text: Sure. Thanks, Kian. So one of the hallmarks of this plan is the level of capital generation. We've talked about that. And really when we talk about an improving profit signature, that's really what we mean. It's this chart here that they've just brought up showing that sort of change to 230 basis points. (slide 71) And in the plan, what we've done is we've meaningfully increased the distribution to greater than £15 billion, but we've also meaningfully, in fact doubled the level of investment. But such is the level of capital generation within the plan. The level of generation actually surpasses both of those two increases. What we've done here is we've deliberately created some capacity for us to be able to invest further if and only if we determine that is the right thing for us to do. And I'll just remind you of our very clear capital hierarchy here and specifically the importance of shareholder returns. So, we're going to set a very, very high bar for any additional level of investment. And quite frankly, if we are unable to find such an investment, then the capital hierarchy will kick in and we will distribute more than we have here in the plan or alternatively, we will be investing more than we have here in the plan and we would expect the momentum of the business in the outer years to be higher than we're presenting here. We have no inclination, no objective here to hold on to higher than required levels of capital but what we're trying to do is create some capacity to underpin some of the meaningful opportunities for growth that we have whilst meaningfully stepping up that level of distribution.

speaker: C.S. Venkatakrishnan
text: I would say, I think if you look at our track record of investment, Anna spoke about the investment which we had made in our prime and financing business and both the quantum of investment and the payback, you saw the quantum of investment in the mortgage broker application platform and the payback. We look to make investments where you would get the revenue realisation fairly quickly and you see that even with Kensington Mortgages and Tesco and "God willing" Best Egg. So, we are looking to do that. And we need to keep that capacity for that reason because opportunities will be there and needs will be there. I would say, Kian, on the second question about subledgers and the sort of the guts of the organisation. You know, it comes from both a philosophical place and from the actual reality of the business. The philosophical place is, as I said, for a long time in this industry, the technology has revolved around the businesses. Now, as you see not just in us, but across the industry, the depth and extent of technology-based services, products, and delivery, the businesses are evolving around technology. And what that means, especially if you're going to take advantage of the promise of new technologies like AI and cloud computing is that you've really got to, harmonise your processes and standardise your approaches. And especially when it comes to data platforms and to the way in which you construct and store your data, the way in which you do computing, the way in which you build models and the way in which you deliver. And if these things are not standard, you add a huge complexity. And so, we've got to unravel that complexity. And in large complex GSIFIs, that's a big task and that's what we are trying to do.

speaker: Alvaro Serrano
text: One of them is kind of a follow-up to the second question maybe for you, Venkat. In one of the slides and you pointed out that 75% of the employees are in support functions. Obviously, at least for me, the surprise of the plan is the cost element as you were referring to. During the plan, how is that number going to come down during the plan in 2028 and beyond that, how low do you think it can go because it's obviously one of the core pillars? And second, maybe a more financial one, on again maintaining the RWAs flat in the Investment Bank and one of the things coming out is ongoing RWA efficiencies. Is there anything - maybe this one is for Anna, but is there anything you can point us to that is pretty mechanical around the way the business is done in Investment Banking, maybe less legacy LBO business, more private credit capital-light businesses, that we can gain conviction that mechanically the RWAs are going to be flat right now? Pointing out to a proportion of contribution today versus three years out, something that will give us confidence that we can keep it flat. Thank you.

speaker: C.S. Venkatakrishnan
text: So first of all, on the cost, just a definitional point. When we call support functions, there's a bit of a legal entity aspect of Barclays. This is what we call Barclays Execution Services. This includes technology and operations, but it also includes compliance, risk, finance, HR, and legal. So it includes basically the non-revenue generating parts or direct revenue-generating parts of the business. So that's the first thing. The second thing, as I've said and I'll have Anna chime in, we don't have an explicit target in terms of number of employees. What I've said is there will be productivity benefits from all these investments. We hope to harness this productivity benefit in improving the quality and delivery of services, whether that is to clients or whether that's internally, right? And there will be obviously a gross efficiency cost-savings that we've outlined and investment in the Group. But we are not outlining a particular people target. I think we are approaching this from something that creates efficiency in order to provide enablement. And then we'll see where we go. Anna?

speaker: Anna Cross
text: If I can just add to that, our real focus from here on in is really on that technology efficiency. So, the majority of cost out, if you like, the efficiency is going to be driven by change delivery, by platform modernisation and the kinds of things that Venkat was talking about, enabling products to market, if you like, much, much faster than we have done before. So that's where we see the sort of meaningful change, if you like in the cost base.

speaker: C.S. Venkatakrishnan
text: It's no accident that the most digitally enabled part of the bank, which is the US Consumer Bank also has our lowest cost income ratio. Right. It's no accident. Go ahead.

speaker: Anna Cross
text: On RWAs, I mean, this is not a new thing for the IB. They've been flat for four years. They were flat for two years before we started the last plan. And whilst we've made considerable progress, 110 basis points [income over average RWA improvement since 2023], we do think that there's more to go here. So let me talk about a couple of stats. The first would be, if you remember when we did our Investment Banking deep dive, we talked about that review of the loan book being really good stewards of capital. We are two-thirds of the way through that review with a third to go. It might be helpful actually if we can bring up a slide that's got the relative revenues over RWAs and you'll really see what's happening in the Investment Bank (slide 64). At the same time, so it's that bottom right hand chart that I'm calling out there. Absolute levels of RWAs have been coming down in banking as we have reviewed that loan book. That's allowed us to be much more nimble in how we deploy RWAs across the Investment Bank and really deploying them at the moment, as you've seen in Markets, just because the market opportunity has been there. The other thing I would call out is much of our growth that we're really leaning on from here on in. Some of the things we talked about before, M&A and ECM, but the International Corporate Bank is a really big part of this part of the plan. It's made tremendous progress in the last two years and that again comes from the treasury coverage model that we talked about in our deep dive. We've increased our deposits by 140% here and now we have the opportunity to really leverage that by deploying the technology that Venkat is talking about and really driving fee products from here. So, we are confident in that trajectory. Venkat?

speaker: C.S. Venkatakrishnan
text: I'll just add to what Anna said. Structurally, it is the International Corporate Bank and Transaction Banking. It is the continued growth in our prime businesses, which revenue per unit RWA because of just the way the lending is structured is generally better. It is over a very long period of time, the way lending and banking has been changing from direct lending on individual credits to portfolio lending. But that's over a very long period of time, but it's the thing Anna said, it's Corporate Banking. It is an emphasis on fee businesses and also you know, at the right points of the cycle, intermediation.

speaker: Guy Stebbings
text: The first question was on capital in terms of targets. You got the 13% to 14% target. I think you've talked sort of running at the top end of that range throughout this plan and given this is the plan now to 2028, post Pillar 2A changes, given the constructive tone from the regulator. I'm just wondering what do we need to see to sort of potentially move lower down in that range as sort of a formal way you're running from the business? Is it just getting that Pillar 2A change from the regulator? And [I assume] you [have] got pretty good visibility as to what you're expecting there. So, if things do land as you expect, maybe you could help sort of frame that and we can think about what that means for capital return and RoTE targets? And then he second question was on the mortgage book in the UK. You referred to the headwind in the first half of this year. Can I just check in terms of the definition of that headwind? Is that sort of a gross headwind? Because I'm mindful that with Kensington and the sort of flow of the book, you might be able to offset some of that as you have some higher LTV, higher margin business coming through. So, can you kind of frame the definition of that headwind? Thank you.

speaker: Anna Cross
text: On the first one, if you go back to the beginning of 2025, what we said was that because we were carrying more Pillar 2 in advance of IRB implementation, you should expect us to operate at the top of the range or towards the top of the range. That's still what we're saying. It's no different to that. And I do expect there to be some pillar 2A offset when we get through Basel 3.1 and IRB. I just don't know what they are right now. What we are trying to do in every single part of this plan is put it in our control. We want our distribution plan to be underpinned by the things that we're doing and that it can't be put of course by the timing of regulatory change or the certainty of that change. That's all we're saying here. So, for us, in the short term, our planning assumption throughout this plan, is that we will be at the top end of the range. Obviously, you should reflect that in the way you think about our distributions, you should reflect that in the way that you calculate our RoTE. But once we get beyond that implementation and we have that clarity, we will, of course, review where we think we should be within that range. We still think that the 13% to 14% range is the right range for Barclays. But at this point in time, we just don't have the regulatory clarity and we want this plan in our control. So that's the reason for it. And on mortgages, I'm specifically talking about a gross impact and it relates to the mortgages that were written at the very end of 2020 and beginning of 2021. As you remember, as we were all coming out of COVID, there was that stamp duty holiday in the mortgage market was very substantial. Those mortgages were written at very widespread, like 160 basis points. That's quite meaningfully different from where we are now. So just as they refinance, you're going to see some relatively short-term pressure across the market as a whole. We think it will be gone by the end of half one [2026]. And then beyond that, you're going to see the kind of progress that you've seen in our NII to date. But it is a growth impact. We're obviously, enjoying very good levels of net lending, driven very much by Kensington and that broker platform. So, it's a short-term hiatus, I would describe it as.

speaker: C.S. Venkatakrishnan
text: And if I may just underline one thing, Anna, whether it's capital or looking at our RoTE, there are potential tailwinds, right? We are planning prudently, but what Anna is referring to, whether it's the new capital rules and what relief we get, there are potential tailwinds. We are not banking on them.

speaker: Ben Toms
text: First one is on Private Banking Wealth Management. What products are you currently missing from your Premier Banking proposition? And how easy is it for you to build those yourself? And then secondly, can you continue on the UK loan book? UK retail banks continue to surprise to the upside on loan book growth relative to GDP. I think your guidance is for 5% loan growth CAGR out 2028. What's driving the growth in excess of GDP? And what's your outlook for volumes in the mortgage market for the next couple of years? Thank you.

speaker: C.S. Venkatakrishnan
text: Let me start on both. We've got a pretty big and complete product suite. There are a couple of gaps in the product suite that are missing, SIPs and Junior ISAs that are coming online. But if you put yourself at a higher level looking at it, starting at the self-directed end of the spectrum, what we've got is Direct Investment, what we used to call Smart Investor, which is you're basically doit-yourself investment buying stocks, bonds. Then you come to the next piece, which is planning and advice. That is where we are doing some work, as I said, to create products, which we will talk to you about soon, which you know clearly constructed, fairly priced, transparently built and efficiently distributed. There we are looking to grow in scale and we've got the basic product set. And then we've got our Private Bank both domestically and internationally. So, I would view it more as a scaling journey than as a completion of product capability. And that is our goal. I think more broadly, the UK is a nation of savers. I think it needs to be more of a nation of investors. I think we're going to have a broader tailwind and support for this. I think it's important role for banks to play and you'll see us emphasise it. Then if I come to loan growth above GDP, let me begin and then Anna should fill in. We've said 5% as you say, loan growth versus nominal GDP of 2%. Basically, there are parts of the business in Corporate Banking, in Business Banking and even parts of personal loans where we were underrepresented in the last number of years. Tesco has given us the capability in personal loans and you can see the increase. You're seeing the increase of 18% growth in lending in the UK Corporate Bank. If you look at the UK Corporate Bank broadly, still loan-to-deposit [ratio of 34%]. So, we have a lot to grow, right, versus what you might normally expect.

speaker: Anna Cross
text: Simply put, Ben, I think it's a combination of increased capability. So, we've talked a lot about the mortgage platform. Actually, we're doing very similar things within the Corporate Banking environment, making it easier for that customer or client to engage with us and making that journey efficient, quick, giving them certainty, etc, that's making a really big difference. I think also the sort of broader product architecture that Venkat talked about. We see it in cards across multiple products. We obviously see it in our mortgage business. So, we're just going to market with a much broader range and certainly more of a step change than we've had sort of two or three years ago. What it isn't is price, and what it isn't is risk. So, you can imagine as CFO, I've got a very keen eye on those things. If you think about our Corporate lending, it's up by 18% year-on-year. We've got more than 1000 new clients in two years. About half of those are driving some of that lending. But as I look at the risk profile, it's not changed since the beginning of the plan. And as I look at the portfolio margin, it's not changed since the beginning of the plan. So, it's really technology, intention to lend, and I would say breadth of product.

speaker: Tim Piechowski
text: I think today, in [your] guidance, it's the first time you've pointed us to the seven-year swap rate from the five-year swap rate on the [structural] hedge book. And could you talk about, is there a change in kind of the duration targeting there and what gives you the confidence to make that change? You're looking at deposit betas, etc?

speaker: Anna Cross
text: We actually extended the length of the hedge last year and taking it from roughly three years to three and a half and that's why the seven-year swap rates becomes the most relevant rate. That really follows the observation of customer and client behaviour, because what we do is every single month, we are looking at how the deposit books perform across Retail and Corporate at a very, very granular level. And what we were observing was really that the customer and client lives were lengthening out and we were getting more confidence around that. So, it's purely a reflection of that change.

speaker: Andrew Coombs
text: So on the Investment Bank, if I look at your 2026 targets, previously you had a greater than 12% target. It's now circa 12%, a high-50s cost income ratio is now circa 60%. I'm assuming the change is primarily due to FX, but perhaps you could firstly confirm? Secondly, when I go back two years and think of the original plan, a lot of the revenue growth was assumed to come from market share gains and you actually assumed a fairly flat wallet. Actually, what's materialised is a much better wallet than you expected, but flat market share. So perhaps you could also just talk to competitive dynamics and how that's played out versus what you thought two years ago and how that then fed through to your 2028 assumptions as well. Then on the US Consumer Bank, I just wanted to understand some of the moving parts because you talked about greater than 13% NIM for 2026 full year, but I think in your earlier commentary, you said 12.5% for Q1, 14% for the second half post the [American Airlines] sale. So, presuming it's the 14% you would argue we should be thinking about into the outer years. But then similarly on the loan-loss ratio charge, you're actually assuming that's coming down even as the exit NIM is higher. So perhaps you could just square the circle there. Thank you.

speaker: Anna Cross
text: Thank you. So, Andy, you are correct. The material moving part between the last plan and this plan is we previously planned on [GBP/USD of] 1.27. We're now planning on [GBP/USD of] 1.35. Now that has no impact on group capital, no impact on our ability to distribute, but in particular, pockets of the bank, you see some concentrated effects and the Investment Bank is one of those, you're going to see it in US Consumer Bank as well. So that movement in FX is worth about 50 basis points. So, all we're doing is we're just truing up our expectations. We're pleased with the progress that it's made so far. I'm not going to mark-to-market that plan every single passing quarter. It's just that as we're resetting targets, we felt like it was the appropriate thing to do. Thank you.

speaker: C.S. Venkatakrishnan
text: I think, on the other side, what I would point to is, on the Investment Bank side, Banking per se, as I said to you, we would like to see greater fee share. What you've seen so far is progress from the hires and the investments we've made, and you've seen greater revenues, obviously and excellent capital discipline. As we make these investments; we hope to see the fee share. On Markets, I would point you to the fact that in the three focus businesses, we've done what we said we would do and we've done it a year early. And as well as the number of our top five clients among the top 100 clients for whom we are top five, that has gone from 30 to 50 to 60. So, there is structural progress being made in these elements.

speaker: Anna Cross
text: Thank you. So Andy, you're right. There's a lot going on in US Consumer Bank in 2026, specifically being driven by the fact in Q2 we expect to exit the American Airlines partnership and also complete the purchase of Best Egg in the same quarter (slide 96). Firstly, that has a NIM impact. I expect the NIM to go to around 12.5% in the first quarter. What's driving that? Well, it's just the accounting that I called out earlier. It's a movement between non-NII and NII. Then we've always said that because American Airlines was such a high-quality portfolio, the NIM on it is relatively low, but also the loan loss rate on it is relatively low. So taken together, it was a relatively low returning portfolio because it's super prime. So what happens when that leaves the portfolio is the NIM will go up further. So you're right, in the second half of next year, I'm expecting, a clean run-rate of NIM, which looks more like 14%. Now, when I come to loan loss rates, that same impact is going to take us from 400 basis points to 500 basis points, but that will be more than offset by NIM. During 2026 in isolation, what you're going to have is a couple of impairment effects. The first is, if you recall, when we buy something, we bring it all on at Stage 1. So, it has to mature through Stage 2. So, you get what we call stage migration. You're going to get that in the General Motors portfolio. So that's going to elevate impairments slightly. And then for a period of time, we're going to be holding on to some non-performing loans from the American Airlines portfolio that won't go with them on the sale. So those two things together are going to show a little bit of elevation during 2026. So that's why I'm guiding you to around 550 loan loss rate, but ongoing, 14% NIM and 500bps loan loss rate.

speaker: Perlie Mong
text: Thinking about the income guidance at the Group level, so it's greater than 5% CAGR. Within that, obviously, Investment Bank is probably below, and the [US] Consumer Bank is above. And with the UK part also growing volumes and greater than 5%. I'm just trying to think about what does it imply about margins. So in terms of product margin, that is, would you expect more of that income growth coming from the volume side? Are we basically past the point where deposit margin is growing very substantially because of the hedge? And obviously, 2026 will probably be a bit higher because of more of the hedges coming through in 2026. So, in 2027 and 2028, how should we think about the margin piece? And that's number one. And number two, so it sounds like Investment Bank RWAs is going to stay relatively flat because you still expect that to come down to about 50% of the Group by 2028. So roughly speaking, it's not much more to the Investment Bank and the cost guidance at a Group level only modestly growing from now to 2028. That suggests [the] Investment Bank not getting very much cost either. So, I'm just trying to think about why you've decided to do that in the context that obviously, the Investment Bank probably is one of the businesses that has performed above expectations in the last cycle. And increasingly there are questions about with the US peers investing more and putting more capital behind Investment Bank, why would you choose not to do so?

speaker: Anna Cross
text: So how do we think about product margin in the UK is I think your question. So, look, there's a bit more to go here and you can see that from the, can we go to the structural hedge slide, please? Thank you. (slide 64). We are assuming that we are going to be reinvesting the structural hedge at 3.5%. The maturing yield over the next three years is materially below that. So, 1.5%, 2.1%, 2.7%. So, you're going to have a considerable hedge tailwind across at least this plan, probably beyond. And everything that we've done around the tenure of the hedge and extending it from 3% to 3.5% is only going to increase that momentum for longer. So that remains there as a, if you like an underpin for product margins. Then if you think about lending more and particularly within our credit card business, all of the volume that we've written over the last two years coming to maturity from its promotional balances, that will start to increase the interest-earning lending in the credit card book. So, we expect those things to continue. speaker: Anna Cross
text: Good question. Thank you. We do think of ourselves on either side of the Atlantic, certainly in retail terms as different things. And originally started as the card business in the US, but now what you've seen is us adding a digital savings platform and now digital unsecured lending. So, pulling that together and being very partner-focused with a broad representation. So, it's not a bricks-and-mortar business. Interestingly, and I don't think we talk about this so much, bigger than Chase in the UK. It's a substantial business. And we do see opportunities to grow it with that sort of framework in mind. So very digitally led. In the UK, we start from a very different place. In UK Corporate or in Barclays UK, you're talking about very, very strong primary banking relationships, which, as you say, is where I started this discussion. So, you're really trying to bring your customer or your client into your ecosystem and do as much for them as possible. That's very different from the kind of disruptive mindset. We see our strategy from here as being very much a continuation of that. That said, in the UK, it's really important that the app and the pricing are as good as those of our competitors and indeed our customer service. We've made a lot of progress over the last few years. We're now pretty much top of the large banks in terms of customer service, but we don't recognise that as the standard that we need to get to because of some of the disruptors around us. I think of it as remaining true to being a disruptor in the US and in the UK using the disruptive elements around you to make your primary relationship better and better and better.

speaker: Edward Firth

speaker: Anna Cross
text: It does make sense. Thank you for that. So, Ed, I mean, we can come back to you with the math on each part of that block. But the way I think about it is on the structural hedge, you're getting income, but obviously no offsetting asset balances. As you get the other growth coming through, you're going to be getting some income, but quite a big move in the denominator as well. speaker: Edward Firth
text: Do you think that deposit competition is related to the hedge, i.e., that as this hedge is coming through banks are sharing that with deposit customers? speaker: Anna Cross
text: It's a good question. I mean you need to ask who has the hedge. So, there's not actually that many hedges of that scale in the UK, three, maybe four. speaker: Dan Fairclough

speaker: Anna Cross
text: So if you look at our cost flight path, you will determine that I think most of the increase in costs this year comes from Best Egg. speaker: Alvaro Serrano
text: My questions are more on the AI sort of CapEx cycle and if you could help us think through it.
